title: Multivariable Optimization
body:
[[Optimization]] from [[CALCULUS 1]] with more than one input. The criterion is unchanged, "the
derivative is zero at an extremum", but with several variables the derivative is the
[[Gradient]] and a new possibility appears: a point can be flat and be **neither** a maximum nor a
minimum. That is a saddle point, and handling it is most of what this note is.

## Critical points

$$
\nabla f = \mathbf{0} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_x = f_y = 0
$$

Every [[Partial Derivative]] vanishes at once, so solve the system. This is the multivariable
version of $f'(x) = 0$ and, as there, it finds candidates rather than answers.

## The second derivative test

Build the **Hessian**, the [[Matrix]] of second partials, and take its [[Determinant]]:

$$
H = \begin{bmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \\ f_{yx} & f_{yy} \end{bmatrix},
\qquad D = \det H = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2
$$

| Condition | Verdict |
|---|---|
| $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} > 0$ | local **minimum** (bowl) |
| $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} < 0$ | local **maximum** (dome) |
| $D < 0$ | **saddle point** |
| $D = 0$ | test fails, no information |

The Hessian is symmetric by Clairaut's theorem, so $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ and $D$ is well defined.

**$D < 0$ is the case with no one-variable analogue**: $f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2$ at the origin is a
minimum along the $x$-axis and a maximum along the $y$-axis, so it is flat but extremal in neither
sense. A gradient-based algorithm sitting exactly on a saddle will not move, which is a real
failure mode in [[Gradient Descent]] and not a curiosity.

## The same criterion from linear algebra

$D$ is the determinant of a symmetric matrix, so the test is really a statement about its
[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|eigenvalues]]: both positive gives a minimum, both negative a
maximum, opposite signs a saddle, and $D = \lambda_1\lambda_2$ is why the determinant detects the
last case. That is definiteness of a [[Quadratic Form]], covered in
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]], and the two courses arrive at one criterion from opposite
directions. In $n$ variables the determinant test stops being enough and the eigenvalue statement
is the one that generalises.

## Absolute extrema on a closed region

Same shape as the closed-interval method, with the boundary now a curve rather than two points:

1. Find critical points **inside** the region
2. Find the extrema **on the boundary**, either by parameterising it or by
   [[Lagrange Multipliers]]
3. Evaluate $f$ at every candidate from both steps, biggest and smallest win

Step 2 is where the work moved. In one variable the boundary was two numbers to plug in; here it is
an entire constrained optimisation problem, which is why the next note exists.

## Where this goes

**Training a model is this note with a million variables.** The [[Loss Function]] is $f$, the
weights are the inputs, and no closed form solves $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$, so [[Gradient Descent]]
walks downhill instead. Second-order methods (Newton's) use the Hessian directly, which is why they
converge in fewer steps and why nobody uses them at scale: the Hessian of a million-parameter model
has $10^{12}$ entries. [[Least Squares]] is the happy exception, a quadratic objective whose
critical-point equation is linear and solvable outright.
